doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Taking up clarinet, alto and flute; first jazz flutist
summary: Lessons with Louis Arfine, adding flute, and his claim to have brought bebop phrasing to the flute.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah there you go. Did you take up the clarinet or the saxophone first, or was it the flute?

I took up, I guess I was eleven I believe when I had a few clarinet lessons. They used to have a teacher on 48th Street, Louis Arfine. And so I started the clarinet and then came the alto I believe and then you have to play the flute to get into the bands so I started the flute, and it seemed not too many people were playing jazz on the flute, and that was around the nineteen fifty something area.
You’re right. There seems to be a little bit of controversy, but you hear different stories of who actually was the first jazz flute player. Your name always comes up. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Yeah my name seems to come up. I understand there could have been some others that I don’t know their playing or I don’t know who started first, but Waymon Carver and some other people.
I think it’s more — they maybe just used it incidentally. So who was the first person to really—

It seems like I was one of the first ones that used it kind of in the bebop way, and mostly from absorbing some of the Charlie Parker and the bebop saxophonists, and just transferring it to the flute.
